name: Tetris
miniText: Why can simple falling-piece rules create difficult sequential decisions? NetLogo Tetris drops tetrominoes into a finite well, permits translation and rotation, removes completed rows, and increases speed with progress. Breukelaar and colleagues [1] analyze the complexity of generalized offline Tetris, Szita and Lörincz [2] learn playing policies through noisy cross-entropy search, and Demaine and Demaine [3] study related polyomino-packing complexity. The baseline illustrates geometric constraints and the delayed consequences of each placement. Rotation conventions, piece sequence, available preview, starting debris, and scoring determine the actual task. Formal hardness on scalable boards with known future pieces does not make every human game equally difficult or establish the complexity of this fixed implementation. High scores from one strategy are performance observations under particular rules, rather than proof of optimal play.
